text: CardioSim Lab. From cardiac electrophysiology to the twelve-lead ECG, recorded live from the running simulator.
Here is one normal heartbeat, in slow motion. The heart, the torso, the ECG and the action potentials all share one clock.
The sinus node fires. It is too small to see on the ECG.
Activation spreads across the atria, from right to left, and builds the P wave.
The AV node delays conduction. That pause is the flat PR segment.
Then the impulse races through the His bundle, the bundle branches and the Purkinje network.
The ventricles depolarise, septum first, then the free walls. This is the QRS complex.
During the plateau almost every cell is depolarised. Gradients are small, so the ST segment is flat.
Recovery is uneven. The epicardium recovers first, and these recovery gradients write the T wave. So the QT interval spans the whole heart, not one cell's action potential.
Now, how a limb lead sees the heart. Lead two looks from the left leg. Lead A V R looks from the right arm.
At every instant, the heart's electrical vector is projected onto each lead axis.
Activation points down and to the left. That is positive in lead two, and negative in A V R, which roughly mirrors it.
The T wave follows exactly the same rule.
The chest leads, V one and V six, are measured against the Wilson central terminal.
They sit close to the heart, so the whole lead field matters, not just a single dipole.
The septum activates from left to right: a small r wave in V one, and a small q wave in V six.
Then the left ventricle dominates: a deep S wave in V one, and a tall R wave in V six.
Next, a premature ventricular complex. An ectopic focus in the left ventricular wall fires early.
No P wave comes before it, and activation spreads slowly from cell to cell, so the QRS is wide.
Repolarisation follows the abnormal order, so the ST segment and T wave point opposite to the QRS.
The impulse also travels backwards into the AV node, so the next sinus P wave is not conducted.
The result is a fully compensatory pause, produced by the simulation itself, not by a stored waveform.
Now two runs, side by side. A is normal. In B, the left bundle branch is blocked. Nothing else differs.
In B, the septum is activated from the right, so the small septal q waves disappear.
The left ventricle is reached slowly, through muscle, which widens the QRS to about one hundred and forty milliseconds.
Repolarisation follows the late activation: a secondary change in the ST segment and T wave.
Now the cellular level. We block half of the rapid potassium current, I K r, in a detailed human ventricular cell model.
The action potential lengthens in every cell type, most of all in the M cells.
The change is mapped onto the tissue model and applied live.
Beat by beat, the QT interval lengthens, while the QRS stays the same.
The Explain tab reports the measured effect on the ECG.
Every number here is measured from the simulated ECG. This is an educational model, not for clinical use.
CardioSim Lab. Understand the mechanisms behind the waveform.
